summary: Specifies the semantics of a MIDCOM protocol, by which agents interact with middleboxes such as firewalls and NATs. It does not define a concrete syntax or transport. It was replaced by RFC 5189.

plainLanguage.summary: It lists the kinds of requests a program can make to a firewall, such as please open a door, without saying how to word them. A later document replaced it.

questions: how do sessions work in MIDCOM
subtitle: Protocol semantics for agents to request firewall and NAT configuration without specifying how to encode the requests.

tldr.problem: Applications need to dynamically configure middleboxes (firewalls and NATs) at runtime, but there was no unified protocol semantics defining how this communication should work in terms of transaction types, state machines, and message flow.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC specifies the semantics of the MIDCOM protocol, defining session control (establishment and termination), policy rule management (creation and maintenance of filtering rules), and policy rule groups without prescribing the concrete syntax or transport. It covers sessions, policy reserve/enable rules, address handling, and state machines.
tldr.outcome: Concrete MIDCOM protocol implementations can follow these semantics. RFC 5189 later replaced this specification with updated semantics. The work informed subsequent middleware communication standards.

today: RFC 5189 supersedes this document with updated MIDCOM protocol semantics and extensions.

sections.title: MIDCOM Protocol Overview
sections.content:
Middleboxes like firewalls and Network Address Translators (NATs) often need to be dynamically configured by applications at runtime. For example, a peer-to-peer application needs to open firewall pinholes or request NAT address bindings. The MIDCOM (Middlebox Communication) working group defined requirements and a framework for such communication, and this RFC provides the protocol semantics that satisfy those requirements.

This document specifies the semantics of the MIDCOM protocol—how agents interact with middleboxes—in terms of transactions, state machines, and message flows. Importantly, it does not define a concrete syntax or transport protocol. Different implementations can use different encodings (e.g., XML, binary) and transports (e.g., TCP, UDP), provided they implement the specified semantics. This approach allows flexibility while ensuring interoperability at the semantic level.
sections.plainLanguage: This is the instruction manual for how agents and firewalls should talk to each other. It says what happens, but not how to say it. The actual language and protocol come later.

sections.title: Core MIDCOM Concepts
sections.content:
MIDCOM operates using four key concepts: sessions, policy rules, address tuples, and transactions. A session is an authenticated and authorized connection between an agent and a middlebox. Sessions must be established before any policy rule transactions can occur. Sessions are initiated by agents and can be terminated by either party. Both agents and middleboxes can maintain multiple sessions simultaneously.

A policy rule is a binding of actions to conditions. In MIDCOM, the condition specifies a set of packets, and the action is either "reserve" (reserve resources) or "enable" (allow traffic). A policy reserve rule reserves IP addresses and port numbers without immediately changing packet processing. A policy enable rule configures the middlebox to allow or translate packets matching a flow specification. Policy rules are organized into groups to simplify management of related rules.

Address tuples describe communication endpoints: A0 is the internal endpoint, A1 is the middlebox's inside address, A2 is the middlebox's outside address, and A3 is the external endpoint. For a firewall, A0=A2 and A1=A3 (endpoints use real addresses). For a traditional NAT, A1=A3 but A2≠A0 (NAT provides external address). For a twice-NAT, both A1 and A2 are provided by the NAT, so A1≠A3 and A2≠A0.
sections.plainLanguage: A session is like logging into the firewall. Policy rules are "allow traffic from X to Y." Address tuples are the endpoints: where the traffic actually comes from, where the firewall sees it, where the firewall sends it, and where it actually goes.

sections.title: Transactions and Protocol Operation
sections.content:
MIDCOM interactions are organized into transactions, which fall into three types: configuration transactions (agent-initiated requests that change middlebox state), monitoring transactions (agent-initiated requests that only read state), and asynchronous transactions (middlebox-initiated notifications not triggered by the agent).

Session control transactions establish and terminate sessions. The Session Establishment (SE) transaction performs mutual authentication between agent and middlebox in up to two steps, with the middlebox advertising its capabilities (firewall function, NAT types, IP versions, maximum rule lifetimes, etc.). Session Termination (ST) is agent-initiated; Asynchronous Session Termination (AST) is initiated by the middlebox.

Policy rule transactions manage rule lifetime and configuration. Policy Reserve Rule (PRR) reserves addresses and ports without changing packet processing. Policy Enable Rule (PER) configures actual traffic forwarding or blocking. Rule Lifetime Change (RLC) extends or shortens rule lifetimes or deletes rules. Policy Rule List (PRL) and Policy Rule Status (PRS) are monitoring transactions that let agents explore existing rules. Asynchronous Policy Rule Event (ARE) notifications inform agents when rules change state or lifetime.

Policy rule group transactions manage groups: Group Lifetime Change (GLC), Group List (GL), and Group Status (GS). Groups exist implicitly; they have no separate state but are derived from their member rules.
sections.plainLanguage: Three kinds of transactions: the agent asks to set things up, the agent asks what is set up, or the firewall tells the agent something changed. For rules, you can reserve space, turn on forwarding, change how long a rule lasts, or ask what rules exist.

sections.title: Sessions and Rule State Machines
sections.content:
Sessions follow a state machine with states CLOSED, NOAUTH, and OPEN. A session starts in CLOSED. If the agent sends a Session Establishment request without a middlebox challenge (mc=0), and other authentication is provided (e.g., via TLS), the session transitions directly to OPEN. Otherwise, SE request with a challenge transitions to NOAUTH, and a second SE request with the agent's authentication response transitions to OPEN. From OPEN, ST transitions back to CLOSED, and AST or connection loss immediately returns to CLOSED.

Policy rules follow a separate state machine reflecting their lifecycle: a rule is created via PRR or PER (entering "reserved" or "enabled" state), may have its lifetime extended via RLC, and eventually reaches end-of-life and is terminated, notifying affected agents via ARE. Each rule has an owner (the agent that created it), determining which agents can modify it. Middleboxes can enforce access control so agents can only access their own rules or (for an administrator agent) all rules.

One critical property is atomicity: request transactions at the middlebox are never interrupted by other requests arriving from different sessions. Asynchronous transactions, however, may interrupt and terminate request processing at any time. This means the middlebox must serialize configuration requests but can emit notifications independently.
sections.plainLanguage: A session goes from closed to open in two steps (or one if TLS is already protecting it). Rules get created, kept alive, and eventually deleted. Only the owner of a rule (or an admin) can change it. The firewall processes requests one at a time, but can interrupt to tell you something changed.

sections.title: Message Types and Structure
sections.content:
MIDCOM defines three message kinds: request, reply, and notification. Request messages contain an agent-unique request identifier, allowing the agent to match replies. Successful replies return the request identifier and transaction-specific parameters. Failed replies contain only the request identifier and a failure reason (e.g., "authentication failed", "no authorization", "lack of resources").

Notification messages are sent by the middlebox without solicitation. Session Termination Notifications (STN) indicate why a session is closing. Policy Rule Event Notifications (REN) carry a policy rule identifier and remaining lifetime when a rule changes state. Group Event Notifications (GEN) carry a group identifier and remaining group lifetime. Notifications contain a middlebox-unique notification identifier to allow the agent to track them.

The semantics define message parameters and their semantics but not the encoding. A concrete protocol specification must encode these parameters using some syntax (binary, XML, etc.) and transport (TCP, UDP, SCTP, etc.). Different implementations may add extra parameters or combine parameters, provided all semantics-defined parameters are preserved. This separation of semantics from syntax allows diverse concrete protocols to all conform to MIDCOM semantics.
sections.plainLanguage: Every request has an ID so you can match the reply to it. Replies say "yes" with the results or "no" with a reason. Unsolicited messages tell you when something changed. The actual wording and how it travels over the network are left to each protocol.

sections.title: Conformance and Implementation Flexibility
sections.content:
The RFC designates transactions as mandatory (must be implemented by all compliant middleboxes and offered to all authenticated agents) or optional (may be implemented and offered selectively). Session control transactions (SE, ST, AST) are mandatory. Policy rule core transactions (PRR, PER, RLC) are mandatory. Monitoring transactions (PRL, PRS) and group transactions (GLC, GL, GS) may be optional. A middlebox advertises its supported transactions to each agent at session establishment via the capabilities exchange.

Concrete protocol implementations may extend the semantics by adding transactions or parameters for domain-specific needs, or by splitting single transactions into multiple transactions for protocol constraints. The specification provides a minimum necessary subset, and conforming implementations are expected to be a superset of it. Access control is configurable: a middlebox may allow agents to access only their own policy rules, or allow an administrator identity to access all rules. The configuration of authorization is left to middlebox policy, not specified by MIDCOM itself.
sections.plainLanguage: Some transactions every firewall must support (starting a session, creating rules, changing lifetimes). Others are optional (listing rules). Each firewall tells you which ones it can do. Real implementations can add more power if they need it.
